title: The Lion and His Donkey Minister
intro: A minister dies, and the wild beasts come to ask their king who will govern them. Within a month there is a cat playing with a mouse bone at the foot of the throne. Shakib Arslan quotes the whole fable in his memoir of Shawqi. The animal who finally explains what has happened waits until he can speak to the lion alone.

translation: The lion is king of the wastes
and all the desert holds.
1.sharh: The second half brings everything living in the desert under one king. By the end his authority will be tested in the few feet around his seat.

translation: His subjects came to him one day,
humbled to the dust.
2.sharh: The beasts approach as a single body. Their deference gives a measure of how much the announcement is going to cost him.

translation: They said, “Long may you live,
you of the bloodstained claws.
3.sharh: The wish for a long reign is courtly. The bloody claws bring the audience briefly back to the animal to whom everyone is speaking.

translation: The minister is dead. Who now
will govern the beasts of prey?”
4.sharh: The question defines the vacant job. Someone must govern creatures dangerous in their own right, and those creatures have an interest in the appointment.

translation: “The donkey is my minister.
My choice has settled it.”
5.sharh: The king announces his candidate and then gives his reason. Both answers end in “my”. The donkey’s qualifications receive no mention.

translation: They burst out laughing, then said,
“What did he see in the donkey?”
6.sharh: The order matters. The laugh comes before the words, and the beasts have already switched from addressing their ruler to talking about him.

translation: They left him there and flew off
with news to make you laugh.
7.sharh: The subjects disperse with something worth retelling. Their speed carries ridicule out of the royal audience and into the kingdom.

translation: By the time a month had passed,
swift as a night or a day,
8.sharh: A month slips by in the space of a line. The poem leaves out the daily stages of decline so the discovery comes upon king and reader together.

translation: the lion woke to find
his kingdom in ruins.
9.sharh: The ruin is already there when the lion notices it. The next lines let us inspect his court from where he sits.

translation: The monkey on his right,
the dog on his left,
10.sharh: Right and left are the places of attendance at court. Two almost identical phrases arrange the animals around the silent king.

translation: and the cat before his very eyes,
playing with a mouse bone.
11.sharh: The small scrap of prey makes a pointed answer to the opening salute. Even a cat can carry on with its game in this king’s presence.

translation: “Which of my forebears,” he said,
“ever had so little dignity as I?
12.sharh: The lion searches his family tree for an explanation. His own recent decision has yet to occur to him.

translation: Where are my power and my terrible grip,
the awe and the regard I commanded?”
13.sharh: His list moves from what his body can do to what other creatures feel about him. A lion can still have his claws after he has lost their respect.

translation: The monkey came to him in private
and spoke after begging pardon.
14.sharh: The monkey who occupied the place of honour has seen the trouble at close quarters. He takes care to speak privately and to make his candour bearable.

translation: “High as you stand among us,
let your sights be high as well.
15.sharh: “High” does double duty. The first use acknowledges a rank the lion already possesses. The second requires him to exercise judgement worthy of it.

translation: Your subjects take their measure of you
from the measure you took of the donkey.”
16.sharh: The monkey repeats the word for judgement, first the subjects’ and then the king’s. The appointment has given everyone a way to judge the judge.

1.1.2.head: مَلك
1.1.2.meaning: King. The middle vowel of malik drops here to fit the foot.

1.1.3.head: القِفار
1.1.3.meaning: Wastes, stretches of open, uninhabited country.

2.1.3.meaning: Subjects under a ruler’s care, here the beasts who come to court.

2.2.1.head: يَوم
2.2.1.meaning: One day, with no particular date, the storyteller’s way into the episode.

2.2.2-3.head: بِكُلِّ اِنكِسار
2.2.2-3.meaning: “In utter brokenness”, with every sign of submission.

3.1.2-3.meaning: “May you live and endure”, the acclamation with which the beasts gain a hearing at court.

3.2.2-3.head: دامي الأَظفار
3.2.2-3.meaning: “Bloody of claw”, a courtly address that recalls the lion’s kills.

4.1.2.head: الوَزير
4.1.2.meaning: The officer entrusted with the affairs of the realm. His death brings the subjects to court.

4.2.1.head: ساسَ
4.2.1.meaning: Governs, directs the affairs of a community.

4.2.3.meaning: Beasts trained by habit to pursue and kill prey.

5.2.1.meaning: Has settled or decreed. The lion treats his preference as a binding decision.

6.1.1.head: اِستَضحَكَ
6.1.1.meaning: Broke into laughter at what she or they heard.

6.2.2-4.head: رَأى فيهِ
6.2.2-4.meaning: “Saw in him”, found a quality in him that could justify the appointment.

7.1.1.head: خَلَّفَ
7.1.1.meaning: Left someone behind. The subjects go off to tell the story out of the king’s hearing.

7.2.1.head: مُضحِك
7.2.1.meaning: Something that raises a laugh, here the appointment itself.

8.1.4.meaning: Has gone by. The thing that turns away is a month.

8.2.1.head: لَيلَة
8.2.1.meaning: A single night, paired with a day. Its final t is pronounced as the reciter joins it to “or”.

9.2.1.head: مُلك
9.2.1.meaning: Kingship and the kingdom over which it extends.

10.1.3.head: اليَمين
10.1.3.meaning: The ruler’s right hand, a place close to his person at court.

11.2.2.head: عَظمَة
11.2.2.meaning: A single bone left from the mouse. Its final t is audible before the next word.

11.2.3.head: فار
11.2.3.meaning: A mouse. The glottal stop in fa’r is eased to a long vowel in rhyme.

12.2.3.head: الوَقار
12.2.3.meaning: Dignity or gravity that commands respect.

13.1.2.head: اِقتِدار
13.1.2.meaning: Command of the means to act and to have an order carried out.

13.1.3.head: بَطش
13.1.3.meaning: A violent grip, the lion’s power to strike or seize.

13.2.2.head: اِعتِبار
13.2.2.meaning: Standing, the regard others accord him.

14.2.3.head: اِعتِذار
14.2.3.meaning: A request for pardon before speaking unwelcome truths.

15.1.3.head: الجاه
15.1.3.meaning: Rank and influence in the eyes of others.

15.2.3.head: الأَنظار
15.2.3.meaning: Ways of judging, particularly the judgement exercised in choosing an officeholder.

16.1.2.head: الرَّعِيَّة
16.1.2.meaning: The body of subjects. The collective noun gathers the opening crowd together again.
